Not in the US. In Australia and other commonwealth countries, the queen reserves the right to dissolve parliament if there is a gridlock. As far as I know, this was only done once, after a budget failed to be passed. The queen's proxy threatened to dissolve parliament if they didn't get a budget through, and then promptly dissolved it anyway the next day after they passed it anyway. In Australia there's Double Dissolution which allows the Prime Minister to call for an immediate national election for every seat in Parliament if certain conditions are met.

The conditions are that a piece of legislation twice fails to be agreed upon between the House and Senate, provided that the bill originated in the House, at least 3 months passed between rejections in the Senate, and the second rejection occurred in the same or next session as the first rejection.

Note that the Prime Minister is virtually always a sitting member of the House, the only time that a Senator was Prime Minister, he resigned and was elected to the House.
